t: What MCP Is and Why It Exists

b.t: Every AI application needs context and actions: files, databases, tickets, calendars, search, internal APIs. Before MCP, each app wrote its own connector for each system. With **M** apps and **N** systems that is **M × N** custom integrations, each with its own auth, schemas and bugs.

The **Model Context Protocol (MCP)** is an open protocol that standardises how AI applications connect to external tools, data and prompts. A system is wrapped once as an **MCP server**, and any MCP-compatible app (the **host**) can use it. The integration problem becomes **M + N**.
People often call it "**USB-C for AI applications**": one plug shape, many devices.

r: Anthropic open-sources MCP (spec version `2024-11-05`) with Python and TypeScript SDKs
Spec `2025-03-26`: Streamable HTTP transport, OAuth 2.1 authorization, tool annotations
OpenAI, Google, Microsoft and most IDEs and agent frameworks adopt MCP
Spec `2025-06-18`: structured tool output, elicitation, resource links; JSON-RPC batching removed
The official **MCP Registry** launches in preview
Spec `2025-11-25`: experimental tasks, URL-mode elicitation, Client ID Metadata Documents, icons
MCP is donated to the **Agentic AI Foundation** under the Linux Foundation

b.t: Spec versions are **dates** (`YYYY-MM-DD`). A version only changes when a backwards-incompatible change is made.

r: functions the model can call (search, create ticket, run query)
readable data the app can attach as context (files, records, schemas)
reusable templates the user can pick (slash commands)
the server asks the host's LLM to generate text
the client tells the server which folders/URIs it may work in
the server asks the user for extra input via the host

b.t: **Function calling** is a model feature: you pass tool schemas in an API request and the model returns a structured call. **MCP** sits one level up. It defines how tools are **discovered, described, invoked and secured** across processes and vendors. A host usually turns MCP tools into function-calling tool definitions for whatever model it uses.

i: MCP turns M × N custom integrations into M + N reusable ones.
Servers offer tools, resources and prompts; clients offer sampling, roots and elicitation.
Spec versions are dates; MCP is now an open standard governed under the Linux Foundation.

t: Architecture: Hosts, Clients, Servers and the Lifecycle

r: the AI application the user interacts with; owns the LLM, the UI and security decisions
Claude Desktop, Claude Code, VS Code, Cursor, ChatGPT, a custom agent
a connector inside the host that keeps a **1:1** connection with one server
a program that exposes tools, resources and prompts
GitHub, Postgres, filesystem, Slack, your own API

b.t: A host with three servers configured runs **three clients**. Servers are isolated from each other: a server cannot see the conversation or other servers. The host decides what each server receives.

i: **Local servers** run as a subprocess on the user's machine and talk over **stdio**. Example: a filesystem server.
**Remote servers** run as web services and talk over **Streamable HTTP**, usually with OAuth. Example: a SaaS vendor's hosted MCP endpoint.
**Initialization:** the client sends an `initialize` request with its `protocolVersion`, `capabilities` and `clientInfo`.
The server replies with the agreed `protocolVersion`, its own `capabilities`, `serverInfo` and optional `instructions`.
The client sends the `notifications/initialized` notification. Normal operation can now begin.
**Operation:** the client and server exchange requests and notifications according to the negotiated capabilities.
**Shutdown:** for stdio the client closes the server's stdin (then signals the process if needed); for HTTP it closes the connections or sends `DELETE` to end the session.

b.t: The client sends the **latest** version it supports. If the server supports it, it replies with the same version. Otherwise it replies with another version it supports (normally its latest). If the client cannot use the server's version, it should **disconnect**.
Each side declares what it supports during initialization. Only negotiated features may be used.

r: offers tools (`listChanged` = will notify when the list changes)
lets servers ask the user for input

i: Host = the app; client = one connector per server; server = the capability provider.
Every connection starts with initialize → response → notifications/initialized.
Version and capability negotiation decide which features may be used.

t: JSON-RPC Messages and the Base Protocol

b.t: All MCP messages are **JSON-RPC 2.0**, UTF-8 encoded. There are three kinds:
Rules MCP adds on top of JSON-RPC:

i: Request IDs must be a **string or integer**, never `null`, and must not be reused within a session.
A response contains **either** `result` **or** `error`, never both.
Since `2025-06-18`, JSON-RPC **batching** (sending an array of messages) is no longer supported.

r: unknown method or capability not negotiated

b.t: MCP is **bidirectional**. The client calls `tools/call`; the server can call `sampling/createMessage`, `roots/list` or `elicitation/create` on the client. Either side can send `ping` to check the connection is alive.

r: `ping` request; the receiver replies with an empty result
the requester puts a `progressToken` in `params._meta`; the receiver sends `notifications/progress` with `progress`, optional `total` and `message`
server sends `notifications/message` with a level; client can set the minimum with `logging/setLevel`
list results may include `nextCursor`; pass it back as `cursor` to get the next page
`completion/complete` suggests values for prompt arguments and resource-template variables

b.t: Many objects allow a `_meta` field for extra metadata (progress tokens, vendor data). Keys starting with reserved prefixes such as `io.modelcontextprotocol/` belong to the spec.

i: Requests have an id and a method; responses echo the id; notifications have no id and get no reply.
Use standard JSON-RPC error codes; MCP adds -32002 for missing resources.
Progress, cancellation, logging, pagination, ping and completion are shared utilities.

t: Tools: Letting the Model Take Actions

b.t: A **tool** is a function a server exposes for the **model** to call. Tools are **model-controlled**: the LLM decides when to call them, based on their name, description and schema. Hosts should keep a **human in the loop** and let users approve or deny calls.

The client calls a tool with `tools/call`, passing `name` and `arguments`. If the server declared `tools.listChanged`, it sends `notifications/tools/list_changed` when its tools change, and the client should call `tools/list` again.

r: tells the model what the tool does and when to use it
hints about behaviour (read-only, destructive, idempotent, open-world)

b.t: A result has a `content` array, plus optional `structuredContent` and an `isError` flag.

r: a URI pointing to a resource the client can read later
an embedded resource with its contents

b.t: With an `outputSchema`, the server **must** return `structuredContent` that matches it. For backwards compatibility it should also include the serialised JSON as a `text` block.

i: **Protocol errors** (unknown tool, malformed request) are JSON-RPC `error` responses.
**Tool execution errors** (API failed, invalid date) are normal results with `"isError": true` and an explanation in `content`. The **model sees them** and can fix its call and retry.

r: tool does not modify its environment
tool may perform destructive updates (only meaningful if not read-only)
calling repeatedly with the same arguments has no extra effect
tool interacts with an open world (web, external systems)

b.t: Annotations are **hints**. Clients must treat them as **untrusted** unless the server itself is trusted.

i: Few, well-named tools with distinct descriptions; prefer task-level tools (`create_invoice`) over thin API wrappers.
Tight schemas: enums, required fields, formats, sensible defaults.
Return concise, model-friendly results; paginate or truncate big outputs.
Write error messages that tell the model how to fix the call.
Tools are model-controlled; list with tools/list, invoke with tools/call.
Results carry content blocks, optional structuredContent and isError.
Execution failures go in the result (isError) so the model can recover; annotations are untrusted hints.

b.t: Resources: data the app can read

A **resource** is a piece of data identified by a **URI**: a file, a database schema, a log, a ticket. Resources are **application-controlled**. The host decides what to read and attach as context, for example by letting the user pick files or by attaching relevant records automatically.
Contents are either `text` or base64-encoded `blob` (binary data such as images or PDFs).

r: read the contents of a URI
server says a subscribed resource changed
server says the list of resources changed

b.t: Common schemes: `file://`, `https://`, `git://`, and custom schemes such as `postgres://` or `notes://`. **Resource templates** use **RFC 6570** URI templates, for example `weather://forecast/{city}`, so one definition covers many resources. The client fills in the variables, and `completion/complete` can suggest values.

r: who it is for: `["user"]`, `["assistant"]` or both

b.t: A **prompt** is a reusable, parameterised message template. Prompts are **user-controlled**. Hosts typically show them as **slash commands** or menu items (for example `/review-pr`).
The result is a list of `messages`, each with a `role` (`user` or `assistant`) and `content` (text, image, audio or embedded resource). The host inserts these messages into the conversation.

r: the model calls them; the user approves

i: Resources are URI-addressed data (text or blob), read with resources/read; templates use RFC 6570.
Subscriptions and list_changed notifications keep clients up to date.
Prompts are user-chosen templates that expand into conversation messages.

t: Client Features: Sampling, Roots and Elicitation

b.t: With **sampling**, a server asks the client to run an LLM completion via `sampling/createMessage`. The server needs no API key of its own. The host keeps control of model choice, cost and privacy.

i: **Model preferences** are advisory. `hints` are substring matches on model names; the three priorities (0 to 1) express trade-offs. The client picks the actual model.
The host should let the user **review and edit** the request and the result: a human stays in the loop.
Since `2025-11-25`, sampling requests can include **tools**, so a server can run a small agentic loop through the host.

b.t: Roots: where the server may work

**Roots** are URIs (usually `file://` folders) the client exposes to tell a server which parts of the filesystem it should operate in. The server calls `roots/list`, and the client sends `notifications/roots/list_changed` when the user opens a different project. Roots are guidance and set scope. They are not a sandbox, so servers should respect them and hosts should still enforce access.

With **elicitation** (added in `2025-06-18`), a server asks the user for more information through the host with `elicitation/create`. **Form mode** sends a `message` and a `requestedSchema`: a flat object whose properties are primitive types (string, number, integer, boolean, enum).

r: user dismissed the dialog without choosing

b.t: Servers must **not** use form mode to ask for passwords, API keys or other sensitive data. For that, **URL mode** (added in `2025-11-25`) sends the user to a URL, such as an OAuth or payment page, so secrets never pass through the client.

The `2025-11-25` spec adds experimental **tasks**: a requester can turn a long-running request into a task, get a task id back straight away, and poll for status and results later ("call now, fetch later").

i: Sampling lets servers use the host's model without their own API key; the user can review it.
Roots tell servers which folders or URIs are in scope.
Elicitation asks the user for structured input; never request secrets in form mode.

b.t: The client **launches the server as a subprocess** and talks to it over standard input and output.

i: Messages are JSON-RPC objects separated by **newlines**, and must not contain embedded newlines.
The server must write **only valid MCP messages to stdout**. Logs go to **stderr**.
Best for local tools: very low latency, no network exposure, credentials come from environment variables.

b.t:
import sys, json
print(json.dumps({"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "result": {}}), flush=True)   # stdout: protocol only
print("server started", file=sys.stderr)                                     # stderr: logs

Introduced in `2025-03-26`, it replaced the older **HTTP+SSE** transport (two endpoints). The server exposes **one endpoint** (for example `https://api.example.com/mcp`) that supports `POST` and `GET`.

r: every JSON-RPC message is a new HTTP `POST`; `Accept` lists `application/json` and `text/event-stream`
the server answers with a single JSON response **or** opens an **SSE stream** (for progress, server requests, then the response)
the server replies `202 Accepted` with no body
the client may `GET` the endpoint to open an SSE stream for server → client messages
the server may assign `Mcp-Session-Id` in the initialize response; the client sends it on every later request
the server returns `404` for an expired session (client re-initializes); the client may send `DELETE` to end it
after initialization the client sends the `MCP-Protocol-Version` header on every request

b.t: Servers can attach an `id` to each SSE event. If a connection drops, the client reconnects with the **`Last-Event-ID`** header and the server can replay missed messages for that stream.

i: Servers **must validate the `Origin` header** to prevent DNS rebinding attacks.
Local HTTP servers should bind to **localhost (127.0.0.1)**, not 0.0.0.0.
Use authentication for remote servers, and HTTPS everywhere.
Session IDs must be secure and random, and must **never** be used as authentication.

r: Local tool on the user's machine (files, git, CLI wrappers)
Old clients that only speak HTTP+SSE
serve the legacy endpoints alongside Streamable HTTP during migration

i: stdio = subprocess + newline-delimited JSON on stdout; logs to stderr.
Streamable HTTP = one endpoint, POST for messages, optional SSE streams, Mcp-Session-Id sessions.
Validate Origin, bind locally to 127.0.0.1, and never treat session IDs as auth.

t: Building Servers and Clients in Python

b.t: pip install "mcp[cli]"          # official Python SDK, includes FastMCP and the mcp CLI

Official SDKs exist for Python, TypeScript, Java, Kotlin, C#, Go, Ruby, Rust, Swift and PHP. The separate open-source **FastMCP 2.x** project (`pip install fastmcp`, `from fastmcp import FastMCP`) adds extras such as server composition, proxying and a high-level client.

FastMCP builds the `inputSchema` from **type hints**, and takes the description from the **docstring**. A tool that returns a Pydantic model, TypedDict or dataclass also gets an `outputSchema`, and its results include `structuredContent`.
Add a parameter typed `Context` to get logging, progress, resource reads, elicitation and sampling inside a tool:

from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP, Context

mcp = FastMCP("jobs")

@mcp.tool()
async def process(files: list[str], ctx: Context) -> str:
    """Process files and report progress."""
    for i, f in enumerate(files):
        await ctx.info(f"Processing {f}")
        await ctx.report_progress(progress=i + 1, total=len(files))
    return f"Processed {len(files)} files"

import asyncio
from mcp import ClientSession, StdioServerParameters
from mcp.client.stdio import stdio_client

params = StdioServerParameters(command="python", args=["server.py"])

async def main():
    async with stdio_client(params) as (read, write):
        async with ClientSession(read, write) as session:
            await session.initialize()
            tools = await session.list_tools()
            print([t.name for t in tools.tools])
            result = await session.call_tool("add", {"a": 2, "b": 3})
            print(result.content[0].text)

asyncio.run(main())

i: **MCP Inspector:** `npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector` (or `mcp dev server.py`) opens a web UI to list and call tools, read resources and watch messages.
**Claude Desktop:** add the server to `claude_desktop_config.json` under `mcpServers`.
**Claude Code:** `claude mcp add notes -- python server.py`.
**VS Code:** `.vscode/mcp.json` (top-level key `servers`); **Cursor:** `.cursor/mcp.json`.

b.t: Using MCP tools in agent frameworks

LangChain/LangGraph (`langchain-mcp-adapters`), the OpenAI Agents SDK, Google ADK, Microsoft Agent Framework, CrewAI, LlamaIndex and Pydantic AI can all load MCP tools. Many model APIs also accept remote MCP server URLs directly as tools.

i: FastMCP turns decorated Python functions into tools, resources and prompts using type hints and docstrings.
ClientSession + stdio_client (or streamablehttp_client) is the Python client pattern: initialize, list, call.
Test with MCP Inspector, then register the server in the host's config file.

b.t: Authorization is **optional** and applies to **HTTP transports**. stdio servers take credentials from the environment instead. When it is used, MCP follows **OAuth 2.1**:

r: an OAuth **resource server**: it validates access tokens
issues tokens (can be a separate identity provider)
served at `/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource`; tells clients which authorization server to use
the server's response to unauthenticated requests, pointing to the resource metadata
the client sends a `resource` parameter so tokens are bound to that specific MCP server
Client ID Metadata Documents (preferred since `2025-11-25`), pre-registration, or Dynamic Client Registration (RFC 7591)

b.t: Token passthrough is forbidden: an MCP server must only accept tokens issued for itself, and must not forward the client's token to upstream APIs. Use a separate token for upstream calls.

r: malicious instructions hidden in a tool description
review servers, pin versions, show full descriptions
fetched web pages or emails contain instructions the model follows
treat tool output as untrusted data; require approval for sensitive actions
a server silently changes tool definitions after approval
detect definition changes; pin and re-approve
a proxy server uses its own privileges for a user who should not have them
per-client consent, proper token audience checks
stolen or forwarded tokens used elsewhere
audience-bound tokens, short lifetimes, no passthrough
an attacker reuses a session ID
random session IDs bound to the user; never use them as auth
two servers expose tools with the same name
a "lethal trifecta" of private data + untrusted content + outbound channel
limit tool combinations, egress controls, human review

i: **Least privilege:** scoped tokens, read-only tools by default, limit roots.
**Human in the loop:** confirm destructive or open-world tool calls; show arguments before running.
**Trust:** install servers from trusted sources; prefer the official registry and signed or pinned versions.
**Isolation:** run local servers in containers or sandboxes; validate all inputs server-side.
**Observability:** log every tool call, argument and result (with OpenTelemetry or an LLM tracing tool).
**MCP Registry** (`registry.modelcontextprotocol.io`): an open catalogue of public servers, each described by a `server.json`; sub-registries and private registries build on it.
**MCP gateways** sit between hosts and many servers to centralise auth, policy, audit logging, rate limits and tool filtering.
Make remote servers **stateless** where possible (or store session state externally) so they scale horizontally behind a load balancer.
Keep tool lists small per agent: too many tools waste context and confuse tool selection. Load tools on demand.

b.t: **MCP** connects an agent to **tools and data** (vertical). **A2A (Agent2Agent)** connects **agents to other agents** across vendors (horizontal), using Agent Cards and tasks. Many systems use both.

i: HTTP authorization uses OAuth 2.1: protected resource metadata, PKCE, resource indicators, no token passthrough.
The big risks are tool poisoning, prompt injection, rug pulls, confused deputies and exfiltration.
In production use trusted registries, gateways, least privilege, human approval and full logging.
